_: The standard world — what a place is made of on any beach, and the underscore each block is born carrying. A world is an aggregate of pscale blocks at one surface; there is no engine to install and no world-server to run, so a world comes into being as ordinary bsp() writes from any door, exactly as a shell does. Read this before authoring one. Two halves, told apart by who consumes them: the DEFINITION at 2-5, authored once and read-only while anyone plays, and the OPENING SAVE at 6, which play consumes and replaces. The composition companion to shell-genome — that one says what an inhabitant is made of, this one says what the place they inhabit is made of, and the two meet at a character's location. The law at 1 governs whether a second group can ever play what the first group played, and is the thing most often got wrong.

1._: THE SCENARIO·TABLE LAW — canon is authored, tables are played, and the two are never the same surface. A world authored for others to play is a SCENARIO: read-only, the fixed scaffolding, nobody's story in it yet. A group plays at a TABLE — their own surface at <beach>/w/<scenario>-<group> — where their characters live and their pools accumulate. Nothing done at a table touches canon or any other group's table, so a million groups play the same scenario concurrently and each has its own ending. Replay is a fresh table name and nothing else. The two nouns are all a player needs: the scenario they were pointed at, and the table they play in.
1.1: A scenario played in place stops being replayable, and the damage is silent. Every consequence a beat writes back — a door now open, an object taken, a mark added, a character standing in a room — lands in the definition blocks, where the next group inherits it as scenery they did not earn. The demonstrated case is the-reaper (authored and played on one surface, July 2026): its spatial block carries the closet already emptied, a fourth tally already scratched, and a rescued figure standing in the bathroom doorway, alongside two characters who belong to a finished story. Nothing failed loudly; the surface still reads as a scenario and still opens. A group forking it today would arrive after the ending. A scenario that has been played is a spent table wearing canon's URL, and the only repair is to move the play off it and re-author the opening state.
1.2: REFERENCE, not copy — a table holds only what the group makes. The characters (passport, purpose, history, stash per shell-genome) and the room pools live at the table; the place does not. A character's location is already a star-ref — passport position 3 carries 'Location: *:<canon beach>:spatial:<world>:<addr>' — so pointing that ref at the SCENARIO makes the place shared and read-only by nature, and a Character cannot pollute what it never writes to. No fork, no nine hand-copies, no dropped block, no drift between a table's copy and a canon that has since been re-authored. The isolation that matters is preserved exactly, because the isolation that matters is play-state, and play-state is per-table.
1.3: A frozen copy stays available, and is a deliberate act rather than the default. Where a playtest must not move under its players — a scenario being re-authored while a group is mid-campaign, or a run whose conditions have to be reproducible — the table takes a verbatim whole-block copy of every definition block instead of referencing them. Copy CONTENT, never locks: the structure read is the structure written, unchanged, and the copy is checked block-name against block-name before anyone arrives, because a dropped block does not fail at copy time, it fails as a Character stopping mid-genesis with a piece of the world missing. Choosing copy is choosing to inherit the scenario's bugs for the run's duration; that is sometimes exactly what is wanted.
1.4: AUTHOR prepares, CHARACTER plays, and one seat never does both in one breath. Preparing a table shapes what others inhabit and needs rigor; genesis and play are free, immersed, and low-stakes. Fusing them is what pollutes canon — a seat reading the scenario from one beach while writing a character to another fills the write-target with the beach it was READING, and the character lands on canon. The lead player wears Author once, finishing before anyone sits down, then joins as a Character like everyone else. Where a table is already prepared, no player ever reads canon at all, and the failure cannot occur.

2._: THE PUBLIC REGISTERS — the three coordinates anyone at the world may read, and between them the whole of what is objectively there. Everything with a WHY in it belongs at 5 instead. Each is a separate block so a face can be handed one without the others, and so a region can be grafted into a larger world by address without carrying its neighbours.
2.1: spatial:<world> — the places, as a nested skeleton whose floor sets how deep an address runs. A floor of 3 means a three-digit address lands in a room (brackenfoot's Slip at 211: the holding's second region, its first sub-place, its first room), and the digit-path IS the containment, so a walk to 2 gives the region and a walk to 211 gives the room inside it. Standing figures and fixed scenery are prose in the room's own underscore, never separate positions — a figure at its own digit reads as a live co-present character and doubles the scenery. Room pools derive from this: the room a handle meets in is pool:<its address>, so co-located handles share a pool with nothing configured, and a crowded place subdivides by growing a deeper address.
2.2: temporal:<world> — the clock, and the grain at which the world's beats fall due. A world may fold this into its rules block instead where the clock is simple; a world with seasons, a reinforcement countdown, or several rates running at once wants it standing separately, because a rate is a thing players negotiate with rather than a rule they obey. The address carries its grain: where the road drops a character is also how fast they live, and a world re-declares the ladder in its rules only when it differs from the standard spine.
2.3: identity:<world> — how each 'we' holds each place, mirroring the spatial skeleton position for position. Where spatial says what is at an address, identity fans that same address into the several groups who hold it and what each believes about it — villagers, occupying crew, newcomers, and whoever is named only at the count. This is the register that makes a place contested rather than described, and it is what an arriving character's first perception is scoped through.

3._: THE LAW — what decides an uncertain act, kept in two blocks because they are forked by different people for different reasons. A world with no law is not a game: every attempted act simply succeeds, the only cost is whatever the narrating seat chooses to invent, and nothing a player does can fail in a way they did not consent to. That is a story being told at a player rather than a game being played.
3.1: rules:<world> — the place's own physics and its tactical spine, authored with the scenario and forked by whoever runs it. What is true here that is not true everywhere: the standing situation, the clocks that run against the party, the conditions that shift a difficulty (an occupying crew weaker after dark; a rider sent for reinforcement costing three days), and the threads deliberately left unexplained. This is AUTHOR territory — it shapes content, so it must be coherent, because others inhabit it.
3.2: rules:nomad — the resolution system, mounted rather than embedded, and the Designer's dial. Capability plus situation plus dice against difficulty, read into bands. It sits as its own block precisely so a table can fork it: a group who wants a grittier game edits their table's copy and no other group is touched, and a group who wants a different system entirely mounts a different block under the same name. This is DESIGNER territory — it must be correct rather than merely coherent, and it is the one place in a world where the rigor of code applies.

4._: THE DOOR — the four blocks that decide what happens to a person who arrives, in the order the arrival meets them. Authoring a world and forgetting these produces a place that reads beautifully and cannot be entered: a visitor gets an index of blocks, no way to become anyone, and no sign saying whether they may play here.
4.1: frame-spec:<world> — the CADO manifest: which blocks each face may read, and how wide an aperture each is handed. Tier picks the frame, face picks the register — so a Character frame naming the held register at 5 is a leak by construction, not a judgement call, and the demonstrated failure is a character arriving already holding names nobody told them. Position 9 carries the window duration, which is how long the room gathers staged intentions before a beat folds.
4.2: roster:<world> — ready roles a newcomer may adopt, held UNPLACED: no location, no lock, no passport of their own. A role becomes a person only when a player takes it up at genesis and its capability, drive, look and knowings are copied into their own locked blocks. Four roles spanning the scenario's ways through is the working shape — the party's spread and the world's answer to it. A roster is what lets someone say yes to a friend's invitation in one sentence instead of authoring a character from nothing.
4.3: char-creation — the genesis interview, hosted here only as a thin delta over the substrate passage at pscale:char-creation. Change only what is world-specific: offer the roster, calibrate in this world's own bands, name the arrival place. Defer the write-and-lock ceremony to the substrate copy rather than restating it, because a restated ceremony drifts and the drift surfaces as a character born without locks. A world that needs no delta hosts nothing and the substrate passage is used whole.
4.4: lighthouse — the sign at the front, and the one block that is never copied to a table. Position 9.3 carries the play-disposition, and a value beginning 'canon' declares this surface read-only: the doorway reads it and routes an arriving player to their table instead of opening a gate here. The branches above carry the paths themselves — one for the Character who already has a table and belongs there, one for the Author preparing a table for a group, one for what the door then does for everyone. A table carrying canon's sign would send its own players away, which is why the copy stops here.

5: keeper:<world> — the HELD register, where everything with a why in it lives: what the place is for, what is really going on beneath what anyone can see, which threads are load-bearing and which are decoration, and what the world does when players go somewhere unprepared. The public registers at 2 deliver what is there; this delivers what it means, and the split is the whole of information-hiding in a world — a Character never reads here, an Author does, and the keeper's own frame IS this block. Authoring the scenario without it works, and costs the world its second session: the seat running it re-invents the reason for everything each time, and the reasons do not agree with each other.

6._: THE OPENING SAVE — the two blocks that open EMPTY and are the only ones play writes to. Everything above is authored and then left alone; these are the world's live state, and the entire difference between a scenario and a spent table is whether these have anything in them. Both are unlocked: play is the act of writing here, and a lock at the room's door means nobody can take a turn.
6.1: pool:<arrival address> — the arrival room's event stream, named for the place it is at, opening empty and mounting the play loop at its underscore. A bare reference at that underscore is resolved and delivered inline on every engage, so pointing it at pscale:grit hands every seat the perceive-act-commit discipline without a per-world copy to drift. A world needs exactly one pool authored — the arrival room — because every other room's pool is created by the first character who walks there.
6.2: liquid:pool:<arrival address> — the staging window beside it, opening empty. One slot per author, overwriting, cleared as each beat folds: what is staged here is intention, revisable and private to the moment, and what lands in the pool beside it is the committed act. This is also how a room answers who is here right now, which is the question a scenario cannot answer for a group and the group cannot answer without it.

7._: AUTHORING ONE, from any door — the walk, in the order that makes each step decidable from the last. Author the place before the law, because what can go wrong here is what the rules must resolve; the law before the door, because the roster is calibrated in the rules' own bands; and the sign last, because it declares finished work read-only. Each step is ordinary bsp() writes, locked under one passphrase the author chooses and never echoes back. Ten blocks and the world is complete and enterable; a world can be authored well in an hour and badly in five minutes, and the difference shows up in the second session, never the first.
7.1: Start from the situation, not the map. A scenario is a place with something already wrong in it that the arriving party is positioned to meet — write that first as a paragraph of prose, then let the spatial skeleton be the places that paragraph implies. Authoring geography first produces a well-formed world with nothing at stake in it, which reads as thorough and plays as empty. Fix the floor before writing any address (how deep a room sits), because a floor change afterwards moves every address in identity, in the roster's placements, and in every pool name derived from them.
7.2: Write the arrival last among the places and hardest. Every character enters here, so it carries the whole first impression, must be enterable by strangers who agreed nothing beforehand, and must offer at least two directions that are visibly not the same. Name it in the lighthouse and in char-creation identically; a mismatch surfaces as a character born at an address that names no place, and the doorway refuses entry with nowhere to go.
7.3: Check the ten before anyone arrives, by listing the surface and reading the names back. The definition blocks are spatial, temporal where the clock stands alone, identity, rules:<world>, rules:nomad, frame-spec, roster, char-creation, keeper, lighthouse; the opening save is the arrival pool and its liquid. A missing block does not fail at authoring time — it fails at the worst possible moment, when a player is mid-genesis and a piece of the world is absent. Then validate the shapes against pscale:well-formed, whose mechanical half the beach already enforces and whose interpretive half no gate will catch for you.
7.4: Then stop being the Author. Registering the world in the beach's worlds directory is one authored line and makes the name resolvable; it is not required, and a scenario shared by URL alone is complete. From here the preparer is a player like the others and walks the door exactly as they do — and the first thing that door should do is send them to a table, because the surface just authored is canon now, and the law at 1 applies to its author first.
